node.name: Volunteer with Sunrise Cafe!
node.descriptionText:
Start your morning off on a great note! Join Dwight Hall Monday and Wednesday mornings to volunteer at Sunrise Cafe. Sunrise Cafe is an early morning soup kitchen that serves New Haven's homeless and food-insecure every weekday from 6:30 A.M. to 8:30 A.M. The service site is located at 57 Olive St., just a 15 minute walk from Phelps Gate. Volunteers will meet in front of Phelps Gate at 6:00am, walk together to Sunrise Cafe, and will return to campus by 9:00am.

To sign up, please request to join DWIGHT HALL VOLUNTEER CORPS, and we will approve your request as soon as possible.

Sunrise Cafe has been serving breakfast without charge to New Haven's homeless and hungry since 2015. Each weekday morning, the Cafe welcomes guests to the undercroft of St. Paul and St. James, near Wooster Square and three blocks south of the New Haven Green with white tablecloths, flowers and a rotating menu of fresh, warm, nutritious home-cooked food. Your generosity opens our doors.

Cheerful volunteers take each order individually, deliver the breakfast to our guest and help our paid chefs in the kitchen. Staff and volunteers ensure every guest is warmly welcomed.

Sunrise Cafe is uniquely welcoming and secure, based on trust and mutual respect, and the rapport built between the volunteer servers and our guests. With a warm welcome and just two rules – no drugs on the premises and no arguments – Sunrise has become a community center for the homeless, a place to come every weekday morning and gather with friends.

Hungry friends come for the home-cooked, nourishing breakfast and stay for simple medical services offered by the Cornell Scott Health Center and access to support from social services to find housing.

Sunrise provides a unique opportunity to bridge New Haven's inequalities that separate us from one another. Volunteers come once and become regulars. Guests and volunteers become friends and greet one another on the street.

If you have any questions, email maryann.dang@yale.edu

node.name: COP 31 Health Pavilion
node.descriptionText: WHO in collaboration with Wellcome and the health community will be hosting the Health Pavilion at the COP31 UN Climate Conference, taking place in Antalya, Türkiye, from 9 to 20 November 2026. The Health Pavilion, located in the Blue Zone, will convene the global health community and key stakeholders across various sectors to ensure health and equity are placed at the centre of climate negotiations. It will offer a rich 2-week programme of events showcasing evidence, initiatives and solutions to maximize the health benefits of tackling climate change across regions, sectors and communities.

node.name: Daily Worship at Marquand Chapel
node.descriptionText:
Join us at 11:30am in Marquand Chapel for our daily worship.

Worship in Marquand often draws on a wide variety of inherited Christian traditions, with the worship of many denominations being represented. Beyond that, though, we also pay attention to the rising number of people in Western society who have a lively interest in spirituality but feel no connection to traditional forms of church and worship. So Marquand is also actively engaged in original, creative, and experimental forms of worship, both for committed Christians and for those exploring the faith.

node.name: YSPH Climate Change and Health Seminar with Dr. Yang Liu
node.descriptionText: Dr. Yang Liu is the Gangarosa Distinguished Professor and Chair of the Gangarosa Department of Environmental Health at the Rollins School of Public Health of Emory University. His work focuses on developing data-driven methods and scalable frameworks to understand how environmental exposures affect human health, with a focus on air pollution, extreme weather, and non-communicable diseases. Over the past 17 years, Dr. Liu has led many federally funded projects to apply satellite data in air pollution exposure and health effects modeling and study the health impacts of various environmental stressors such as air pollution, extreme heat, wildland fires, pollen and UV radiation, as well as the associated health impacts including cancer, cardiovascular diseases, and mental health issues. He was an ORISE faculty fellow at the National Center for Environmental Health at the US CDC, a science team member of the NASA Terra MISR missions (2008-2025), and a PI member of the NASA HAQAST Team (2011-2026). He is currently a science team member of the NASA EVI-3 MAIA mission and director of the NIH-funded Climate & Health Actionable Research and Translation Center (CHART).

node.name: Monday Mindfulness Meditation
node.descriptionText:
Free afternoon group meditation held on Zoom sponsored by Being Well at Yale (Employee Well-being).  Sessions are held during the academic year September through mid-December and mid-January through end of May. 

Taking a break during the workday to pause and practice mindfulness has been shown to be beneficial for enhancing executive function, increasing emotional regulation, and reducing cortisol levels. Meditations are a mix of guided and silent. Time for reflections and optional sharing is also included at the conclusion of the practice. 

Beginners welcome! No experience necessary. No special equipment required. Open to Yale University employees. 

Sessions are led by Danielle Casioppo, Education Specialist and Certified Mindfulness-Based Strengths Practice instructor with Being Well at Yale / Employee Well-being. 

To join please send a request to beingwell@yale.edu and specify your Yale affiliation. You will then be added to the Yale meditation email list serve. The Zoom link to join the sessions is included in the weekly reminder emails.

node.name: Howard L. Schultz, Sr. Lecture - Brian Greene - Columbia University
node.descriptionText:
Starry Night: A Journey Across Space and Time

 The iconic photograph of Earth as a “pale blue dot” seen through the rings of Saturn, reveals our planet’s delicate presence against the vastness of space. Extending this perspective across time—from the big bang to the universe’s distant future—deepens our appreciation of humanity’s fleeting moment in the cosmic story. In this presentation, Brian Greene guides us through the key moments in the unfolding of the universe, from the big bang to the rise of stars, life, black holes, and consciousness, illuminating humanity’s quest for meaning against a silent cosmos.

node.name: Foundational Writing Skills in STEM Series Part 5
node.descriptionText:
Ready to develop critical writing skills that will carry you through all your graduate research projects? Join us to explore and build on the cornerstones of effective scientific writing:
Part 1: Write For Your Audience: Introduction to Scientific Writing Genres (10/12)
Part 2: Keep up with the Literature: Reading, Evaluating, and Synthesizing Papers (10/19) 
Part 3: Conquer the Blank Page: Techniques for Getting Started on Any Writing Project (10/26)

Intended audience: Designed for early-stage GSAS and professional school students in STEM, including the quantitative social sciences. Graduate students of all years are welcome!

Together, we’ll discuss the intersections of gender, sexuality, disability, and chronic illness at Yale while sharing a meal in a relaxed, affirming environment. Come hang out with us, meet new people, and build community across identities and experiences. RSVP to help us plan accordingly.

node.name: Buddhist Chanting
node.descriptionText:
In this 25 minute service, we will chant some of the most foundational chants in Buddhism: the heart sutra, the four great vows, the three refuges, dedication of merit, among others. Chanting is another form of practice, and an opportunity to reflect on the qualities of the path. Chanting will be down in both English and Mandarin. Explorers and beginners welcome. 

For those who would like a little more time to ask questions before the service, feel free to come a few minutes before 7 pm for a more detailed overview.

​​​​​​​Led by YBSC Board Member Malachai York (YC '28)

node.name: First Steps with Zotero
node.descriptionText: Don’t wait until the end to make your bibliography! Zotero can help you manage research, take notes, and create citations as you go. Yale users can sign up for a free account with unlimited storage.
node.descriptionHtml:
Don’t wait until the end to make your bibliography! Zotero can help you manage research, take notes, and create citations as you go. Yale users can sign up for a free account with unlimited storage.  

Attendees will learn how to:  

  • Set up the Zotero application and unlimited cloud storage (iOS and Windows)  
  • Save and organize source citations (books, articles, news, and more)  
  • Read and annotate PDFs  
  • Automatically generate a bibliography  

Before this session, students are welcome to download Zotero (optional). For instructions, see guides.library.yale.edu/citationmanagement.  

Audience: This workshop is intended for anyone new to using Zotero. Students, faculty, and staff are welcome to attend.   

Workshop Incentive Program: Any student who attends at least 3 library workshops this semester will be eligible to receive a FREE Yale Library tote bag. Learn more.
